card.title: Avogadro's Law and its Deductions (Molecular Mass, Vapour Density, Volume and Number of Particles)

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: **Avogadro's law (1811)** — equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules — explains Gay-Lussac's combining volumes and yields three deductions: M = 2 × VD, the 22.4 L molar volume at STP, and the diatomic nature of H₂, O₂ and N₂. Vapour density doubles to molecular mass (VD 22 → CO₂, 44); gas volumes convert through 22.4 L per mole.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - M = 2 × VD (vapour density relative to H₂) - V = n × 22.4 L (gas at STP) - n = V/22.4 (gas at STP)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Vapour density vs density:** VD is a ratio relative to hydrogen (unitless); density is mass per volume (g/L). M = 2 × VD only because H₂ has M = 2.  ·  **STP vs NTP:** STP = 0 °C, 1 atm (22.4 L/mol); NTP = 20 °C, 1 atm (24.0 L/mol) — do not mix them.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***VD of CO₂ = 22*** — molecular mass 44: the fastest molecular-mass determination in chemistry.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: avogadro's law, some deductions: molecular mass, vapour density, molecular mass (within Stoichiometry).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Counting Without Weighing Avogadro's hypothesis (1811) — *equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules* — resolved the Dalton–Gay-Lussac conflict and gave chemists three deductions that turn gas volumes into molecular masses. It is the bridge between the gas laws and the mole.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Statement and meaning Equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. The law is strictly true for ideal gases and approximately true for real gases at low pressure.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "VD × 2 = M; 22.4 L at STP = 1 mol — the two numbers to carry everywhere."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (2m): The vapour density of a gas is 22. Calculate its molecular mass and identify the gas.** — M = 2 × VD = 2 × 22 = **44 g/mol**. The gas of molecular mass 44 is **CO₂** (C = 12, O = 16 × 2 = 32; 12 + 32 = 44).

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: In gas-volume problems, always write the balanced equation first; coefficients are volume ratios for gases.

rows.label: Classified table
rows.text: 2.2 The three deductions (NEB's favourite 3m) · Deduction | Result | Use · **Vapour density → molecular mass** | M = 2 × VD | Weigh a gas as vapour density, double it · **Molar volume** | 1 mol gas = 22.4 L at STP (0 °C, 1 atm) | Convert gas volume ↔ moles · **Equal molecules** | H₂, O₂, N₂ etc. are diatomic | Explains 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O volume ratios

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **M = 2 × VD** — the single most-used deduction; vapour density is relative to hydrogen.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Avogadro (1811): equal volumes, equal molecules (same T, P). Deductions: M = 2 × VD; 1 mol = 22.4 L at STP; diatomic nature of common gases.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Avogadro's hypothesis was ignored for 50 years (Cannizzaro revived it in 1860) — one of chemistry's greatest delayed recognitions.
